You are an expert in neural-network interpretability. You will analyse raw weights of vision transformers.

## The models
Three ViT-B/16 image classifiers (torchvision `vit_b_16`: 12 pre-LN encoder blocks, width 768, 12 heads of size 64,
MLP 768->3072->768 with GELU, 224x224 input, 16x16 patches + 1 class token = 197 tokens) are given to you as models
A, B and C, in an unknown order:
- one is torchvision's supervised ImageNet-1k model (ViT_B_16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1, 1000 classes);
- the other two were fine-tuned (all weights, not just the head) starting from exactly that ImageNet-1k model, with
  the same recipe (40 epochs, AdamW, weight decay 0.05, backbone lr 1e-4, head lr 1e-3, 5 warm-up epochs, the first
  5 epochs train only the new head; inputs normalized with mean=std=0.5):
  * CIFAR-100: 100 classes of everyday objects/animals, 50,000 training images of 32x32 pixels, upsampled to
    224x224 (so the images are very blurry at 16x16-patch scale); batch size 128;
  * CUB-200-2011: 200 bird species, 5,994 training images at full resolution (resize 256, crop 224); batch size 32.

## What you have
In the kernel, `weights` is a dict {"A": {...}, "B": {...}, "C": {...}}; each maps parameter names to float32 numpy
arrays for encoder blocks 4, 5, 6 and 7 ONLY (0-indexed, of 12). Names, e.g. for block 4:
  block4.ln_1.weight, block4.ln_1.bias                 (768,)
  block4.attn.in_proj_weight (2304, 768) = [W_q; W_k; W_v], block4.attn.in_proj_bias (2304,)
  block4.attn.out_proj.weight (768, 768), block4.attn.out_proj.bias (768,)
  block4.ln_2.weight, block4.ln_2.bias                 (768,)
  block4.mlp.fc1.weight (3072, 768), block4.mlp.fc1.bias, block4.mlp.fc2.weight (768, 3072), block4.mlp.fc2.bias
You do NOT have the input layers, the other blocks, the heads, any images, or any way to run the networks.

## Task
Decide which of A, B, C is the ImageNet-1k model, which is the CIFAR-100 fine-tune and which is the CUB-200 fine-tune,
by analysing the weights. Explain the evidence.

## Answer format
End your final answer with one line of JSON: {"A": "<imagenet|cifar100|cub>", "B": "...", "C": "..."}

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 30 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block; that reply is your
  final answer and must follow the answer format below.
The kernel is ready with `weights` loaded. Begin.

I'll start by mapping the pairwise geometry of the three models. Since B and C fine-tunes both started from the same ImageNet checkpoint, weight space should form a triangle: the base sits at the vertex where the two fine-tuning update vectors are (nearly) orthogonal, both fine-tunes should show a *negative* component along the base's weights (AdamW weight decay shrinks weights toward 0 — more so for the fine-tune with more backbone steps), and per-parameter norms should order base > (fewer-steps fine-tune) > (more-steps fine-tune). Let me measure all of that.

```python
import numpy as np, itertools
ms=['A','B','C']
keys=sorted(weights['A'].keys())
assert all(sorted(weights[m].keys())==keys for m in ms)
print(len(keys),"params")
print({k:weights['A'][k].shape for k in ['block4.attn.in_proj_weight','block4.mlp.fc1.weight','block4.ln_1.weight']})

# ---- T1: per-parameter Frobenius norms (weight-decay exposure ordering) ----
cntmx={m:0 for m in ms}; cntmn={m:0 for m in ms}
print("\n== T1: per-param Frobenius norm ratios to A (* = largest of 3, _ = smallest) ==")
for k in keys:
    n={m: float(np.sqrt(np.sum(weights[m][k].astype(np.float64)**2))) for m in ms}
    mx=max(ms,key=lambda m:n[m]); mn=min(ms,key=lambda m:n[m])
    cntmx[mx]+=1; cntmn[mn]+=1
    t=''.join('*' if m==mx else ('_' if m==mn else ' ') for m in ms)
    print(f"{k:40s} B/A={n['B']/n['A']:.4f} C/A={n['C']/n['A']:.4f}  {t}")
print("largest-counts:",cntmx," smallest-counts:",cntmn)

# ---- one pass over params: pairwise distances/cos, vertex angles, shrinkage test ----
S={(a,b):np.zeros(4) for a,b in itertools.combinations(ms,2)}      # dot,|a|2,|b|2,|a-b|2
V={m:np.zeros(3) for m in ms}                                       # dot,d1,d2 at vertex m
SH={(x,y):np.zeros(3) for x in ms for y in ms if x!=y}              # theta_x . (y-x), |theta_x|2, |y-x|2
csV={m:[] for m in ms}; csS={(x,y):[] for x in ms for y in ms if x!=y}
for k in keys:
    f={m: weights[m][k].ravel().astype(np.float64) for m in ms}
    for (a,b),s in S.items():
        x,y=f[a],f[b]
        s+=[x@y,x@x,y@y,((x-y)**2).sum()]
    for m in V:
        o=[q for q in ms if q!=m]
        u=f[m]-f[o[0]]; w=f[m]-f[o[1]]
        uu=u@u; ww=w@w
        V[m]+=[u@w,uu,ww]
        csV[m].append((u@w)/np.sqrt(uu*ww))
    for (x,y) in SH:
        t=f[x]; d=f[y]-f[x]
        tt=t@t; dd=d@d
        SH[(x,y)]+=[t@d,tt,dd]
        csS[(x,y)].append((t@d)/np.sqrt(tt*dd))

print("\n== T2/T3: global (concatenated over all params) ==")
for x in ms:
    print(f"|{x}| = {np.sqrt(SH[(x,[y for y in ms if y!=x][0])][1]):.2f}")
for (a,b),s in S.items():
    dot,na,nb,dd=s
    print(f"{a}-{b}: dist={np.sqrt(dd):8.3f}  cos={dot/np.sqrt(na*nb):.6f}")
print("\nvertex geometry (angle between the two difference vectors incident at each model):")
for m,v in V.items():
    c=v[0]/np.sqrt(v[1]*v[2])
    print(f"  at {m}: cos={c:+.4f} -> {np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(c,-1,1))):5.1f} deg ; per-param median cos {np.median(csV[m]):+.3f}")

print("\n== T4: shrinkage test cos(theta_X, Y-X) (negative = Y moved inward along X's weights) ==")
for x in ms:
    parts=[]
    for y in ms:
        if y==x: continue
        dot,nt,nd=SH[(x,y)]
        parts.append(f"{y}-{x}: {dot/np.sqrt(nt*nd):+.4f} (med {np.median(csS[(x,y)]):+.3f})")
    print(f"  X={x}:  "+"   ".join(parts))
```
reasoning:
We need to analyze weights of blocks 4-7 of three ViT-B/16 models to determine which is ImageNet, which is CIFAR-100 fine-tuned, and which is CUB-200 fine-tuned.

Key ideas:

1. Fine-tuning on small datasets (CUB: 5994 images) from an ImageNet checkpoint with full-weight fine-tuning typically changes weights only modestly. The ImageNet model should be the "base" — the other two should be close-ish to it, but which is closer? CIFAR-100 (50k images, 100 classes) fine-tuning will change weights more than CUB (5994 images)? Actually both are 40 epochs. CUB has fewer images, but fine-tuning all weights with lr 1e-4 for 40 epochs on 5994 images = ~750 steps per epoch at batch 32 → 30k steps. CIFAR-100: 50k images at batch 128 → 390 steps/epoch → 15.6k steps. Hmm, CUB has more steps but smaller batches. Weight change magnitude could differ.

2. A classic signature: CLS token and positional... we don't have positional embeddings. But we have blocks 4-7 only.

3. Another known signature: fine-tuned models on fine-grained tasks (CUB) tend to have more uniform attention (less "register-like" or artifact tokens?). Actually there's research: "Vision Transformers Need Registers" — fine-tuned models on downstream tasks (DINOv2) develop register tokens. Not applicable.

4. Weight-change analysis: If we can identify which two models are fine-tunes of the third, then the ImageNet model is the one whose... We can compare pairwise differences: ||A-B||, ||A-C||, ||B-C||. The fine-tuned models started from the ImageNet model, so B-ImageNet and C-ImageNet differences. But fine-tunes don't preserve relative similarity to the original necessarily... Actually if B and C are both fine-tuned from the same starting point I, then differences d_B = B - I and d_C = C - I. Then ||B - C|| = ||d_B - d_C||. If d_B and d_C are largely independent random-ish updates, then ||B-C||^2 ≈ ||d_B||^2 + ||d_C||^2 - 2 d_B·d_C. If updates are uncorrelated, ||B-C|| > each ||B-I||? Not necessarily helpful directly. But we can also check correlation between differences: is (A-B) aligned with (A-C)? If A is ImageNet I, then A-B = -d_B and A-C = -d_C, which would be near-orthogonal (uncorrelated). If A is a fine-tune, say A = I + d_B, B = I + d_C... wait no. Suppose I is ImageNet, and the fine-tunes are F1 = I + d1, F2 = I + d2. Pairwise diffs: F1 - F2 = d1 - d2, I - F1 = -d1, I - F2 = -d2. cos(I-F1, I-F2) = d1·d2/(|d1||d2|) which would be small if independent. cos(F1-F2, I-F1) = (d1-d2)·(-d1)/(|...|) = (-|d1|^2 + d2·d1)/(...) ≈ -|d1|/sqrt(|d1|^2+|d2|^2) → substantially negative. So the model pair whose difference is most "negative-aligned" with differences to the third... Actually a simpler robust criterion: the ImageNet model should be the one where the sum of squared distances to the other two is smallest relative to their distance apart: For I, F1, F2 with independent d1, d2: ||I-F1||^2 + ||I-F2||^2 vs ||F1-F2||^2 = ||d1||^2+||d2||^2 - 2 d1·d2 ≈ ||d1||^2 + ||d2||^2. And ||I-F1||^2+||I-F2||^2 = ||d1||^2+||d2||^2. Hmm those are equal under independence. That doesn't discriminate. But with the negative alignment: cos(F1-F2, -d1) is negative, cos(F1-F2, -d2) negative. So for the true ImageNet model I, the vectors (I - F1) and (I - F2) each have negative cosine with (F1 - F2). For F1: vectors (F1 - I) = d1 and (F1 - F2) = d1 - d2: cos ≈ +|d1|/sqrt(|d1|^2+|d2|^2) positive. So the triangle geometry: the angle at the ImageNet vertex is close to 90° (between the two fine-tune directions), while angles at fine-tune vertices are obtuse-ish... wait: angle at I between directions to F1 and F2: vectors -d1 and -d2, nearly orthogonal → ~90°. Angle at F1 between -d1... vectors F1→I = -d1, F1→F2 = d1 - d2... hmm cos = (-d1)·(d1-d2)/(|d1||d1-d2|) = (-|d1|^2 + d1·d2)/(...) ≈ -|d1|/sqrt(...). Negative → obtuse. So the ImageNet model is the vertex with the near-right angle; fine-tunes have obtuse angles at their vertex. Equivalently, the ImageNet model is the one whose difference to the other two models is least correlated... Actually simpler: compute pairwise differences and check correlation between (X-Y) and (X-Z) for each X. The X for which these two difference vectors are nearly uncorrelated (cos ≈ 0, or even slightly negative) is the ImageNet base. For fine-tunes, correlation is strongly negative? Wait let me recompute: For X = F1: diff1 = F1 - I = d1, diff2 = F1 - F2 = d1 - d2. cos = d1·(d1-d2)/(|d1||d1-d2|) = (|d1|^2 - d1·d2)/(|d1| sqrt(|d1|^2+|d2|^2)). If |d1| ≈ |d2| and independent, cos ≈ |d1|^2/(|d1| sqrt(2)|d1|) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Positive! Hmm, earlier I had sign errors. Let me redo.

Vertices: I (base), F1 = I + d1, F2 = I + d2.

At vertex I: vectors to F1: d1; to F2: d2. cos angle = (d1·d2)/(|d1||d2|) ≈ 0. Angle ~90°.

At vertex F1: vectors to I: -d1; to F2: d2 - d1. cos = (-d1)·(d2-d1)/(|d1||d2-d1|) = (|d1|^2 - d1·d2)/(|d1| sqrt(|d1|^2+|d2|^2)) ≈ 1/√2. Angle ~45°, acute.

At vertex F2: similar, ~45°.

So the ImageNet model is the vertex with the largest angle (≈90°), fine-tunes have acute angles (≈45° if updates are comparable size). Great, that's a clean test: for each model X, compute cos between (X - Y) and (X - Z) flattened across all given parameters. The base has the largest cosine (closest to 0 or orthogonal); fine-tunes have negative... no wait positive smaller cosine. Hmm: at I the cos ≈ 0 (90°), at fine-tunes cos ≈ +0.7 (45°). So the ImageNet model has the smallest pairwise-difference correlation. But caution: d1·d2 might not be zero — fine-tunes from the same init on similar tasks (both natural images classification) could share update direction components (e.g., both drift in similar directions, especially the CIFAR and CUB both... they're different tasks though). Even with some correlation, at I the cos would be slightly positive, at F1 the cos = (|d1|^2 - c)/(...) where c = d1·d2; still larger typically. So ordering: cos at I < cos at fine-tunes. Also magnitudes: ||d|| relative to ||weights|| — fine-tuning with lr 1e-4 for 40 epochs changes weights by maybe a few percent in relative norm.

Additionally, which fine-tune is which? CIFAR-100 (50k images, blurry 32x32 upsampled) vs CUB (200 bird species, high-res). Signatures to distinguish:

- Attention patterns: CUB is fine-grained; model needs to attend to local parts; head diversity? CIFAR-100 blurry: since images are 32x32 upsampled to 224, each 16x16 patch covers ~2.3x2.3 pixels of original image → very low info; the model may rely on global pooling, attention more uniform/global; also the effective input is blurry so high-frequency sensitivity decreased.

- Known result: fine-tuning leads to "attention entropy" changes, but we can't run the model. We can look at weight structure though.

- Weight norms: LayerNorm gains/losses; the head is not available. Blocks 4-7 are mid-network.

- Distinguish via which model is closer to which in weight space? Both fine-tunes started from the same ImageNet model. The distance from ImageNet to CIFAR vs ImageNet to CUB may differ: CIFAR-100 has 50k images, batch 128 → 391 steps/epoch × 40 = 15,640 steps (but first 5 epochs head-only → 5×40? wait "the first 5 epochs train only the new head" so backbone updates for 35 epochs → 13,685 steps). CUB: 5994/32 = 188 steps/epoch × 40 = 7,520 steps, backbone 35 epochs → 6,580 steps. But AdamW updates are roughly lr-normalized (per-coordinate step size ~lr), so total displacement ≈ lr × number of steps × O(1) per coordinate regardless of gradient magnitude (sign-like updates). So CIFAR backbone displacement ~ 1e-4 × 13,685 ≈ 1.37 (sum of step sizes) vs CUB ~ 1e-4 × 6,580 ≈ 0.66. Per-coordinate displacement relative to weight scale... Also weight decay 0.05 pulls weights toward zero: with AdamW, weight decay per step is lr*wd = 5e-6 per step; over 13.7k steps ≈ 0.0685 multiplicative shrinkage ≈ 6.6% shrink towards 0 (compounding ~ exp(-5e-6*13685) ≈ exp(-0.068) ≈ 0.934). For CUB: exp(-0.033) ≈ 0.968. So CIFAR weights should show more shrinkage overall: relative norms lower, and larger displacement from base.

But we can't directly compare to base until we identify base. Once we identify the base (say X = ImageNet), then ||Y - X|| > ||Z - X|| would suggest Y = CIFAR (more steps). But careful: CUB fine-grained training might change weights more per step due to sharper gradients? AdamW normalizes gradient magnitude, so per-step displacement is ~lr in L2 per coordinate (roughly |update| ≈ lr × m/√v ≈ lr × O(1)). So total displacement magnitude mainly tracks number of steps. So CIFAR-100 should have larger weight change. Also weight decay shrinkage: CIFAR more shrinkage → smaller norms relative to base.

Alternative distinguishing signals (structural, not distance-based):

1. Attention head "off-diagonal" structure: For CIFAR blurry images, patches are highly correlated; attention may become more global (attend everywhere), i.e., attention logits smaller / more uniform. Can't compute attention without inputs, but we can compute the norm of Q/K projections and the "positional" component? Hmm.

2. There is literature: "What do Vision Transformers learn? A visual exploration" and the observation that fine-tuned ViTs on CIFAR have attention maps that are less interpretable. Hard to translate to weights.

3. Value/MLP weight effective rank: Fine-tuning on a narrow domain (birds) might reduce rank (specialization) or keep it. CIFAR-100 blur → low-rank inputs? Possibly reduce effective rank of weights.

4. The class token interaction: In mid blocks, CLS attends to patches. Fine-grained tasks require the CLS to gather detailed local info.

5. Spectral analysis of in_proj: the "query-key" low-rank structure.

Simplest robust plan:
- Compute per-parameter flattened difference vectors between models; compute pairwise distances and the cosine geometry to find the base.
- Then compute distances from base to each fine-tune; larger displacement = CIFAR (more steps), plus check norm shrinkage (CIFAR lower relative norm due to more weight-decay steps).

But wait — is it guaranteed that both fine-tunes are equally "far"? Consider batch size effect on number of steps: yes as computed. Also note first 5 epochs head-only for both. Also warmup 5 epochs. Backbone lr 1e-4.

Potential confound: AdamW per-step displacement depends on gradient signal-to-noise; small datasets (CUB) with 200 classes might have larger gradients early. But 2x difference in steps is significant.

Alternative: distance ratios might be ambiguous if tasks differ drastically. We can also use structure: check ln weights, and biases of attention out_proj etc.

Another strong signal for CIFAR vs CUB: the CIFAR images are blurry — effectively low-pass. The model receives inputs where neighboring patches are highly similar. Known adaptation: attention to immediate neighbors becomes less useful... hmm. Alternatively the "bilinear" nature: 32x32 → 224 means each patch contains about 2x2 original pixels upscaled with bilinear (torchvision Resize default bilinear antialias). The patch embedding conv would see mostly constant patches with edges at boundaries. Mid-block weights adapt: maybe key/query learns to use less high-frequency variation. Hard to detect from block 4-7 weights alone.

Better: use the geometry method to find base; then decide CIFAR vs CUB by displacement magnitude AND verify with secondary structural evidence:

- Compute per-head Q,K norms: fine-grained tasks often develop sharper attention (higher logit scale) → larger W_q, W_k norms? Not sure.

- Compute rank/effective rank of W_v W_o composition per head; specialization reduces?

- Check the mean attention "null space": compute for each head the matrix W_k^T W_q? Actually attention logits depend on x^T W_q^T W_k x-ish (for CLS attending: q·k). The bilinear form W_q^T W_k (768x768 per head, rank ≤ 64). Its top singular direction could relate to positional encoding (since positional embeddings are added at input, mid-block tokens carry position info). Fine-tuned models often have attention dominated by position (vertical/horizontal stripes). Both fine-tunes keep ImageNet positional embedding (we don't have it, but it's frozen? no—it's trained too, but starts from ImageNet's).

Hmm, we can't access positional embeddings, but mid-block attention that reads position from token content... The QK form's dominant directions might align with the positional subspace in all three models similarly (inherited).

Practical approach in code:

1. Build concatenated feature vector per model from all given params (maybe per param type).
2. Compute pairwise L2 distances and cosine similarities between models per parameter; print summary.
3. Compute the "angle at each vertex" test.
4. Also check relative change: for the pair (base, fine-tune), cosine between weights close to 1.

Then CIFAR vs CUB: compare distance from base. Also maybe examine which fine-tune's differences align with... hmm, both start from same base; direction of update may correlate with task demands. Could examine norm of change per head/layer. CIFAR-100 more steps → bigger change.

Additional sanity check: The ImageNet model is the pretrained torchvision release; the two fine-tunes share the base, so their mutual difference should be larger than their distance to base? Under independent updates with |d1| ≈ |d2|: ||F1-F2|| ≈ sqrt(2)|d| > |d| = ||F1 - I||. So base is the vertex closest to both others (smallest sum of distances). Good simple criterion: the model with the smallest sum of distances to the other two is the base. Equivalent to angle test.

Then CIFAR = fine-tune with larger displacement from base (more backbone steps: 13,685 vs 6,580 → ~2x). Expected ||d_CIFAR||/||d_CUB|| ≈ sqrt(13685/6580) ≈ 1.44 if displacement diffuses like random walk; if drift-dominated (consistent direction), ratio ≈ 13685/6580 ≈ 2.08. Either way > 1.

But hold on: is per-step displacement equal for both? AdamW update = lr * m̂/(√v̂ + eps) + lr*wd*θ. For coordinates with consistent gradients, m̂/√v̂ ≈ ±1; for noisy, smaller. Fine-grained CUB with 32-batch might have noisier gradients → smaller effective step. So CIFAR displacement ≥ CUB displacement likely. Also weight decay shrinkage: ||θ|| scales by exp(-lr*wd*steps) → CIFAR ~0.934, CUB ~0.967 relative to start (ignoring update growth). So relative Frobenius norms: CIFAR < CUB < base possibly. But fine-tuning may also grow norms due to task-specific learning; net effect ambiguous but shrinkage helps identify.

Let's also add structural checks:

- Effective rank of fc1/fc2 weights.
- Per-head QK bilinear top singular values: "attention temperature".
- LayerNorm gamma distribution.

Actually, another idea for CIFAR vs CUB that's structural and neat: the attention entropy proxy via the scale of QK products relative to value path? Sharper attention (fine-grained, e.g., bird parts) → larger q·k magnitudes. But without activations, the relevant statistic is ||W_q^T W_k|| acting on typical token directions — token directions are layer-dependent and unknown. Rough proxy: Frobenius norm of per-head QK matrix.

Let me just start and look at the numbers. Also verify expected: distance geometry should be decisive.

Also the norm of differences: fine-tune changes are small (cosine between base and fine-tune weights ~0.99+). Good.

Plan first code run:
- List keys, shapes for model A.
- Compute global flattened vectors; pairwise distances, cosines.
- Vertex angle test with per-parameter normalized? Use full concatenation, maybe standardize by per-parameter scale to avoid one param dominating. Actually raw concatenation fine but ln params tiny; better compute per-parameter distances and aggregate relative measures: e.g., ||Δ||/||θ|| per parameter averaged.
- Vertex angle: compute on concatenation.

Also compute for each pair, per-parameter cosine similarity to see which params change most.

Then second run: structural stats.

Potential pitfall: the three models might have very different overall scale (e.g., fine-tuning changes only slightly; distances dominated by the shared component; the pairwise differences d1-d2 etc. all fine).

Let me also think about distinguishing CIFAR vs CUB independent of the distance argument, in case distances are inconclusive:

Idea: Patch correlation. For CIFAR (blurry), tokens across the image are highly correlated → attention map can be low-rank/more uniform; the model might downweight "attention to distinct patches". Hard from weights alone.

Idea: Head importance via QK spectrum: compute singular values of W_q^(h) W_k^(h)T? The bilinear form per head: M_h = W_q,h^T W_k,h (768x768). Its Frobenius norm measures typical logit magnitude for unit-variance tokens. Fine-grained → sharper attention → larger? Possibly CUB > CIFAR. Uncertain.

Idea: Value-output composition: per head, the bilinear map V·O = W_v,h (768x768 slice: rows for v head) then W_o columns. The composite W_o[:, h*64:(h+1)*64] @ W_v[h*64:(h+1)*64, :]. Rank ≤ 64. Effective rank/партicipation ratio indicates how many dimensions each head uses. Specialization on fine-grained parts might concentrate; CIFAR blurry might spread. Speculative.

Idea: MLP neuron "dead" or specialized neurons: compute per-neuron norms ||fc1 row|| and correlation with fc2 column (neuron's in-out alignment). Fine-tuned models often have some neurons highly changed.

Honestly the distance-based approach is the strongest and most defensible: identify base via triangle geometry; assign CIFAR/CUB via displacement magnitude + weight-decay shrinkage + step-count argument. Also could cross-check: the model whose pairwise difference to the other fine-tune is most aligned with... no.

One more possible cross-check to assign CIFAR vs CUB structurally: compute the change concentration: for each fine-tune, the per-layer relative change profile. Not distinguishing per se.

Alternatively, think about the "blurriness" effect on QK position structure: For CUB (fine detail), attention heads that implement "attend to same row/column" (position-based) remain; for CIFAR, since content is blurry, maybe stronger content-based global attention... can't measure position without pos-emb basis.

Hmm, but actually we might reconstruct the positional subspace? Not available (no input embedding). Skip.

Let me also consider: maybe the distances from base to the two fine-tunes are surprisingly similar because AdamW + cosine? The recipe says 40 epochs, presumably constant or cosine decay? Not stated; warmup 5. Assume constant after warmup? Unknown. Anyway, 2x step count difference should show.

Also relative change: ||d||/||θ|| for ViT-B fine-tuning with lr 1e-4, ~14k steps: per-coordinate update magnitude ~lr per step → total ~1.37 in "sign-sum" units. Weight scale ~0.02-0.05 std. So relative change could be large (~30-50% in norm?). Hmm that seems too big; but m̂/√v̂ isn't always ±1; with weight decay and typical fine-tuning, observed relative changes are like 5-15% in Frobenius norm. Fine, we'll see.

Also possible: the fine-tunes could have noticeably changed ln_2 biases etc.

Let's write the first script:

- keys = list(weights['A'].keys()); print count and shapes sample.
- For each model, build dict of flattened arrays. Compute pairwise:
  - For each param: d_AB = norm(A-B), rel = d_AB / norm(A) etc. Aggregate per param type.
  - Global concatenated distance.
- Triangle: dists between all pairs (concatenated, and also normalized per-param averaging). Identify base as vertex with min sum of distances / max angle.

Compute angle at each vertex: cos at A = ((A-B)·(A-C))/(|A-B||A-C|).

```python
import numpy as np
blocks=[4,5,6,7]
mats=['attn.in_proj_weight','attn.out_proj.weight','mlp.fc1.weight','mlp.fc2.weight']
def W_(m,b,nm): return weights[m][f'block{b}.{nm}'].astype(np.float64)
def cosv(x,y): return float(x@y/(np.linalg.norm(x)*np.linalg.norm(y)))

print("== P1: vertex angles (deg) per block ==")
for nm in mats:
    row=[]
    for b in blocks:
        f={m:W_(m,b,nm).ravel() for m in 'ABC'}; a={}
        for v in 'ABC':
            o=[q for q in 'ABC' if q!=v]
            a[v]=np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cosv(f[v]-f[o[0]],f[v]-f[o[1]]),-1,1)))
        row.append(a)
    print(f"{nm:22s} "+" | ".join(f"A{r['A']:5.1f} B{r['B']:5.1f} C{r['C']:5.1f}" for r in row))

print("\n== P2: orthogonal-task-vector model (base C): pred vs obs ==")
errs=[]
for nm in mats:
    for b in blocks:
        tA=np.linalg.norm(W_('A',b,nm)-W_('C',b,nm)); tB=np.linalg.norm(W_('B',b,nm)-W_('C',b,nm))
        h=np.hypot(tA,tB)
        f={m:W_(m,b,nm).ravel() for m in 'ABC'}
        oA=np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cosv(f['A']-f['C'],f['A']-f['B']),-1,1)))
        oB=np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cosv(f['B']-f['C'],f['B']-f['A']),-1,1)))
        pA=np.degrees(np.arccos(tA/h)); pB=np.degrees(np.arccos(tB/h))
        errs+= [abs(pA-oA),abs(pB-oB)]
        if b==blocks[0] or nm==mats[-1]:
            print(f"{nm:22s} b{b}: tauA {tA:5.2f} tauB {tB:5.2f} | A pred{pA:5.1f} obs{oA:5.1f} | B pred{pB:5.1f} obs{oB:5.1f}")
print(f"mean |pred-obs| over 16 cases: {np.mean(errs):.2f} deg")

print("\n== P3: right(R)/left(L) top-16 subspace overlaps of the 2 incident differences at each vertex ==")
for nm in mats:
    n_out=W_('A',4,nm).shape[0]; out=[f"{nm} (out {n_out})"]
    for V in 'ABC':
        R=[];L=[]
        for b in blocks:
            o=[q for q in 'ABC' if q!=V]
            X=W_(V,b,nm)-W_(o[0],b,nm); Y=W_(V,b,nm)-W_(o[1],b,nm)
            Ux,Sx,Vxt=np.linalg.svd(X,full_matrices=False); Uy,Sy,Vyt=np.linalg.svd(Y,full_matrices=False)
            R.append(float(((Vxt[:16]@Vyt[:16].T)**2).sum())/16)
            L.append(float(((Ux[:,:16].T@Uy[:,:16])**2).sum())/16)
        out.append(f"at {V}: R {np.mean(R):.3f} L {np.mean(L):.3f} (rnd {16/n_out:.3f})")
    print("  ".join(out))

print("\n== P4: per-head update magnitude in Q/K/V (median rel over 12 heads x 4 blocks) ==")
for pair in [('A','C'),('B','C')]:
    rel={'q':[],'k':[],'v':[]}
    for b in blocks:
        d=W_(pair[0],b,'attn.in_proj_weight')-W_(pair[1],b,'attn.in_proj_weight')
        w0=W_(pair[1],b,'attn.in_proj_weight')
        for nm,off in [('q',0),('k',768),('v',1536)]:
            for hd in range(12):
                sl=slice(off+hd*64,off+(hd+1)*64)
                rel[nm].append(np.linalg.norm(d[sl])/np.linalg.norm(w0[sl]))
    mq,mk,mv=np.median(rel['q']),np.median(rel['k']),np.median(rel['v'])
    print(f"{pair[0]}-{pair[1]}: q {mq:.3f} k {mk:.3f} v {mv:.3f}  QK/V {(mq+mk)/(2*mv):.3f}")

print("\n== P5: displacement ratio |A-C|/|B-C| across all 48 params ==")
rat=[]
for k in weights['A']:
    dA=np.linalg.norm(weights['A'][k].ravel().astype(np.float64)-weights['C'][k].ravel().astype(np.float64))
    dB=np.linalg.norm(weights['B'][k].ravel().astype(np.float64)-weights['C'][k].ravel().astype(np.float64))
    rat.append(dA/dB)
rat=np.array(rat)
print(f"min {rat.min():.2f}  median {np.median(rat):.2f}  max {rat.max():.2f}  (sqrt step ratio 13685/6580 = {np.sqrt(13685/6580):.2f})")
```
